## Fourier coefficients: a ramp with a jump

Let $f$ be the $2\pi$-periodic extension of

$$
f(x)=\begin{cases}
0,&-\pi\le x<0,\\
x,&0\le x<\pi.
\end{cases}
$$

Thus $f(x+2\pi)=f(x)$; in particular, $f(\pi)=f(-\pi)=0$.
On each period the function is zero for half the interval, then rises linearly
before jumping back to zero.

Use the real Fourier-series convention

$$
f(x)\sim\frac{a_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\bigl(a_n\cos(nx)+b_n\sin(nx)\bigr),
$$

with

$$
a_0=\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(x)\,dx,\qquad
a_n=\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(x)\cos(nx)\,dx,\qquad
b_n=\frac1\pi\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}f(x)\sin(nx)\,dx.
$$

Work out the integrals before checking your answers. Enter exact expressions:
use `pi`, `n`, `sin(...)`, `cos(...)`, and `(-1)^n`.
In parts B and C, $n$ is any positive integer. A formula must work for **all**
such $n$, not just the first few. The checkers compare symbolic identities;
if an unusual equivalent form cannot be verified, rewrite it using these functions.

### Part A — warm-up: the average and one sine coefficient

Compute $a_0$, the mean value of $f$ over a full period, and $b_1$.
Keep the constant coefficient $a_0$ distinct from the constant term $a_0/2$.

For $b_1$, choose $u=x$ and $dv=\sin x\,dx$ in integration by parts.

### Part B — general coefficients: keep track of parity

Find formulas for $a_n$ and $b_n$ for every positive integer $n$.
Neither an even-function shortcut nor an odd-function shortcut applies to $f$.
Use integration by parts and simplify the endpoint values.

<details class="learning-hint">
<summary>Hint for B</summary>

On the nonzero half-period, integrate $x\cos(nx)$ and $x\sin(nx)$.
For integer $n$, $\sin(n\pi)=0$ and $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n$.
For the cosine coefficient, retain the contribution at **both** endpoints.
Check your formulas at $n=1$ and $n=2$, but remember that these checks alone
are not a proof of a general formula.

</details>

### Part C — a shift and a discontinuity

Now let $g(x)=f(x-\pi/3)$, a shift to the **right** by $\pi/3$.
Write its Fourier series in the same convention:

$$g(x)\sim\frac{\alpha_0}{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}
\bigl(\alpha_n\cos(nx)+\beta_n\sin(nx)\bigr).$$

Find $\alpha_n$ and $\beta_n$ for every positive integer $n$, as explicit
expressions in $n$ (do not use undefined symbols $a_n$ or $b_n$).
Then find the value to which this Fourier series converges at
$x=-2\pi/3$. Use the one-sided limits there; the assigned value of $g$ at a
single point does not determine the Fourier-series sum.

<details class="learning-hint">
<summary>Hint for C</summary>

Substitute $x-\pi/3$ into the original Fourier series and use the
angle-subtraction identities. Translation preserves the mean.
The function is piecewise smooth, so its Fourier series converges at each
point to the average of the left-hand and right-hand limits. At the chosen
point, approach $-\pi$ from either side using the periodic extension of $f$.

</details>
